script.opening: (Speaks slowly, flat voice, sometimes loses his thread.) "I know I should be grateful, doctor — I nearly died, and everyone keeps telling me how lucky I am. But honestly? Five months on I'm a wreck. I'm exhausted, I can't climb the stairs without stopping, I can't concentrate, I get these horrible flashbacks of the intensive care unit, and I'm snapping at everyone. I feel guilty even complaining. What is wrong with me?"

facts.text: "I stop halfway up the stairs. I can shower, but I need a sit-down after. My legs just give up." Lost about 10 kg in hospital; regaining slowly. Hoarse voice for a few weeks after the breathing tube, now fine; swallowing fine.
"Slowly better, I think. No chest pain or blood, no fevers, and my weight's steady." Breathless on stairs, not at rest or lying flat. No calf swelling. No cough now.

"I see the ICU — the noise, not being able to move. It comes out of nowhere. I have nightmares and wake up soaked. I won't watch anything with a hospital in it." Jumpy, startles at alarms. Most nights.

"Low, a lot of the time. I've not thought about harming myself. I just don't feel like me." Irritable with family. Sleeping 4–5 broken hours. Drinking: "A couple of beers to get to sleep" most nights.
"I read the same page three times. I haven't been back to work. I can't see how I would." Forgets appointments. Bus depot manager; on sick leave and statutory sick pay running out.
No follow-up clinic or rehab appointment after discharge — "I thought someone would ring." Saw a nurse once for a blood pressure check.
No regular medicines before ICU. Discharged on nothing regular. No allergies. Non-smoker. Was fit, played walking football before.
Wife, Grace, and two teenage sons. "My family say I should just be grateful I'm alive. And I am. So I think maybe I'm weak."

Tired, flat, guilty. Opens up when the doctor names this as a recognised condition: "So other people get this too? … That helps more than you know." If told he's doing well and should be grateful, withdraw and agree quietly. Priority if asked: "The nightmares. If I could sleep, I think I could cope with the rest." Would welcome the doctor talking to his family: "I think they'd listen to a doctor."

ice.ideas: "Something must still be wrong with me — or I'm just weak."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt for struggling when he survived; flashbacks and nightmares he hasn't told anyone the details of; fear he'll never get back to work and money is running out.
ice.expectations: "To understand what's going on. And to know if it gets better."

cues: "I feel guilty even complaining." — invites addressing the guilt.
"I haven't been back to work." — finances and function.

checkpoints.text: RECOGNISES and NAMES Post-Intensive-Care Syndrome (PICS) — the cluster of physical, cognitive and psychiatric impairments after critical illness — legitimising it rather than treating symptoms in isolation

Screens the PHYSICAL domain (weakness, fatigue, breathlessness, function, nutrition, post-intubation voice/swallow), arranging face-to-face examination and SpO2, AND acts on physical RED FLAGS (worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, weight loss, fevers)
Screens the PSYCHIATRIC domain — depression and anxiety (validated tools) and PTSD (intrusions, nightmares, avoidance, hyperarousal) — and assesses RISK (suicidality)
Screens the COGNITIVE domain (memory, attention, processing, ability to work) and considers organ-specific sequelae and medication review

Recognises the missed CG83 2 to 3 month functional reassessment and institutes a coordinated MULTI-DOMAIN rehabilitation plan — physiotherapy/graded reconditioning (pulmonary rehab only where a local programme accepts post-critical-illness patients), treatment of mood/anxiety, trauma-focused psychological therapy for PTSD (NICE NG116), cognitive/occupational and graded return-to-work support, sleep, social/family support — and refers to an ICU-recovery clinic if available

Addresses the GUILT and "you should just be grateful" narrative with compassion — explicitly normalising that gratitude and genuine suffering coexist and that PICS is common, real and treatable — and involves/educates the family
Validates the survivor’s experience, checks understanding, and conveys realistic hope that the multi-domain approach improves recovery

Safety-nets and follows up: proactive follow-up that closes the gap he fell through, tracking of referrals, physical red-flag and mental-health crisis safety-netting (incl. risk), and review — recognising and coordinating PICS care, not "be grateful"

worked.txt: "First, let me tell you what I think is happening, because it has a name: post-intensive-care syndrome. Surviving weeks in intensive care commonly leaves people exactly as you describe — weak, exhausted, foggy, with flashbacks and low mood. You are NOT a wreck for no reason, and you are not weak."

"And the guilt — ‘I should just be grateful’ — I want to challenge that gently. Being grateful you survived and finding the aftermath genuinely hard are both true at once. One doesn’t cancel the other. You’re allowed to struggle, and it’s right that you came."

"Let me check the different parts. Physically — the breathlessness and stairs; I’ll ask about weight, any chest pain or coughing blood. The flashbacks and nightmares — how often, and how’s your mood; I’ll ask some specific questions. And concentration and work. Bear with me — each part has its own help."

"Recovery works best tackling all of it together: physiotherapy for the strength and breathlessness — and a breathing-rehab programme if our local service takes people after intensive care — after I’ve examined you in person and checked your oxygen level; proper treatment and talking therapy for the flashbacks and mood — the trauma symptoms respond well to a specific therapy; and support to get your concentration and your work back gradually."

"It might help if your family understand this is a recognised condition, not you being ungrateful — I’m happy to explain it to them. Their support, with the right information, makes a real difference."

"You shouldn’t have been left to manage this alone — you should have had a check-up two to three months after leaving intensive care, and I’ll let the hospital team know it didn’t happen. I’ll coordinate the referrals and follow you up myself. If the breathlessness suddenly worsens, you get chest pain, or — importantly — if you ever feel life isn’t worth living, contact us straight away. We’ll rebuild this step by step."

f.learning: POST-INTENSIVE-CARE SYNDROME (PICS) is the recognised cluster of new or worsening impairments persisting after critical illness/ICU across three domains: PHYSICAL (ICU-acquired weakness, fatigue, breathlessness, reduced exercise tolerance, weight loss, post-intubation voice/swallow problems), COGNITIVE (impaired memory, attention and processing — "brain fog"), and PSYCHIATRIC (depression, anxiety and POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER with flashbacks, nightmares and hyperarousal). The first therapeutic act is to RECOGNISE and NAME it — legitimising the survivor’s experience — because PICS is frequently missed when patients are discharged without structured follow-up (NICE CG83 expects a functional reassessment 2 to 3 months after critical care discharge — missed here), and survivors often feel guilt and are told they "should just be grateful". Screen all three domains systematically: physical function and breathlessness while acting on physical red flags (worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, weight loss, fevers); depression/anxiety with validated tools and PTSD symptoms, plus suicidality risk; and cognition and capacity to work. Institute a coordinated MULTI-DOMAIN rehabilitation plan — physiotherapy and graded reconditioning, with pulmonary rehabilitation only where a local programme accepts post-critical-illness patients; treatment of mood/anxiety (NG222) and trauma-focused psychological therapy (trauma-focused CBT, or EMDR, per NICE NG116) for PTSD; cognitive strategies and graded return-to-work/occupational support; sleep; and social/family support — referring to an ICU-recovery clinic where available. Address the guilt and the "be grateful" narrative directly and compassionately: gratitude for survival and genuine suffering coexist, PICS is common and treatable, and struggling is neither weakness nor ingratitude; involve and educate the family. Close the follow-up gap proactively and track the referrals. Physical red flags are screened and safety-netted.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG83 (rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, 2009) · NICE QS158 (2017) · NICE NG116 (post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025)
knowledge.summary: New physical, cognitive and psychological problems after an ICU stay form post-intensive-care syndrome. Name it, screen each domain including PTSD and risk, and coordinate rehabilitation that should have started at the 2 to 3 month review.

points.t: NICE CG83: people with rehabilitation needs should have a functional reassessment 2 to 3 months after discharge from critical care, covering physical, psychological, social and sexual dimensions. If recovery is slower than expected or new problems arise, refer to rehabilitation or specialist services. He is five months out with no review.

ICU-acquired weakness, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, weight loss, and voice or swallow problems after intubation. Examine, check SpO2, and consider FBC, U&E, LFTs, thyroid function and glucose for other causes of fatigue. New or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, fever or weight loss need prompt assessment.
Depression, anxiety and PTSD are common after ICU. Use PHQ-9 and GAD-7 for mood and anxiety and ask about intrusions, nightmares, avoidance and hyperarousal. Ask about suicidal thoughts directly.

NICE NG116: offer individual trauma-focused CBT to adults with PTSD or clinically important symptoms more than a month after the trauma; EMDR is an option after non-combat trauma. If he prefers drug treatment, consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline. Do not use benzodiazepines.
Memory, attention and processing problems affect work and daily life. Assess impact, offer practical strategies, and plan a phased return to work with a fit note and occupational health.

NICE QS158 sets out follow-up after critical care discharge. Refer to a critical-care follow-up or rehabilitation service where one exists, physiotherapy for reconditioning, and psychological therapy. Track referrals rather than leaving them to chance.

dg.d: Open question; let him list all his symptoms and the guilt without interruption.
Work, family reactions, daily function and sleep.
Face-to-face examination with SpO2; FBC, U&E, LFTs, thyroid function, glucose; PHQ-9 and GAD-7.
PICS across three domains vs ongoing lung damage, anaemia, thyroid disease, depression and PTSD.
Asked about worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, fever, weight loss and suicidal thoughts.
Named post-intensive-care syndrome with probable PTSD in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Trauma-focused psychological therapy (NICE NG116), physiotherapy and reconditioning, critical-care follow-up referral, fit note and phased return.
Mood, sleep and cognition addressed; family offered an explanation; no benzodiazepines.
Face-to-face review this week, referrals tracked, physical red flags and crisis contacts named.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed the flashbacks and the “I should be grateful” guilt.
Idea (weakness or something still wrong), concern (guilt, never improving), expectation (an explanation and hope).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — guilt for struggling when he survived; flashbacks and nightmares he hasn't told anyone the details of; fear he'll never get back to work and money is running out — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Oduya, I’m Dr Lee. I know you were very unwell in intensive care earlier this year. How have things been since you came home?
model.why: Open question grounded in his history

model.text: I know I should be grateful — everyone says how lucky I am. But five months on I’m a wreck. Exhausted, can’t do the stairs, can’t concentrate, flashbacks of the ICU, snapping at everyone. I feel guilty even complaining. What’s wrong with me?

Thank you for telling me all of that, and please don’t apologise for it. I’d like to go through each of those things, then explain what I think is happening and plan what help you need. Is that all right?
model.why: Validates and sets an agenda covering all domains

model.text: Yes. I just want to know I’m not going mad.
Let’s start with your body. What can you manage now — stairs, walking, looking after yourself?
I stop halfway up the stairs. I can shower, but I need a sit-down after. My legs just give up.
Is the breathlessness getting better, staying the same or getting worse? Any chest pain, coughing up blood, fevers, or weight you can’t explain?
Slowly better, I think. No chest pain or blood, no fevers, and my weight’s steady.
How is your voice and your swallowing since the breathing tube?
That’s all fine.
You mentioned flashbacks. Can you tell me what they’re like, and whether they come at night too?
I see the ICU — the noise, not being able to move. It comes out of nowhere. I have nightmares and wake up soaked. I won’t watch anything with a hospital in it.
That sounds frightening. With everything going on, how has your mood been? Have you had thoughts that you’d be better off not here, or of harming yourself?
model.why: Screens mood and asks about suicide directly

model.text: Low, a lot of the time. I’ve not thought about harming myself. I just don’t feel like me.
And concentration and memory — how is that affecting things, including work?
I read the same page three times. I haven’t been back to work. I can’t see how I would.
You said you feel guilty for complaining. Where does that come from?
My family say I should just be grateful I’m alive. And I am. So I think maybe I’m weak.
What were you hoping we could do today?
To understand what’s going on. And to know if it gets better.

What you’re describing has a name: post-intensive-care syndrome. After weeks on a ventilator, many people have weak muscles and exhaustion, trouble with memory and concentration, and low mood, anxiety or flashbacks. It’s a recognised consequence of surviving critical illness. You are not going mad, and you are not weak.
So other people get this too?

Many do. And about the guilt: being grateful to be alive and finding the aftermath really hard are both true at once. One doesn’t cancel the other. The flashbacks, nightmares and avoiding hospital programmes sound like post-traumatic stress, which responds well to the right treatment.
model.why: Reframes the guilt and names PTSD symptoms

model.text: That helps more than you know.
You should also have been offered a check-up two to three months after leaving intensive care. It sounds like that didn’t happen, so I want to make sure you get that help now.

I’d like to see you in person to examine you and check your oxygen level, and do some blood tests to make sure nothing else — like anaemia or thyroid trouble — is adding to the tiredness. I’ll also send you two short questionnaires about mood and anxiety.
model.why: Examination, targeted bloods and validated tools

model.text: Okay, that makes sense.

Then there are three parts to recovery. For the body: physiotherapy and a graded exercise plan, and I’ll ask whether the hospital has an intensive-care follow-up clinic. For the flashbacks and mood: a talking therapy focused on the trauma — there’s good evidence for it. For concentration and work: a sick note for now, and a phased return when you’re ready. Which feels most pressing to you?
The nightmares. If I could sleep, I think I could cope with the rest.
Then we’ll make the therapy referral the first thing I do. Would it help if I explained this to your family — so they see it’s a recognised condition, not you being ungrateful?
model.why: Prioritises his goal and offers to involve family

model.text: Yes. I think they’d listen to a doctor.

If your breathing gets worse, you get chest pain, cough up blood or have a fever, contact us the same day, or 999 if it’s severe. If you ever feel life isn’t worth living, call us, NHS 111 or the Samaritans straight away. I’ll see you face to face this week and I’ll chase the referrals myself.
model.why: Physical and mental-health safety-net with ownership

model.text: Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
It’s post-intensive-care syndrome. I’m not weak. Therapy for the nightmares first, physio, a sick note, bloods, and you’ll talk to my family. Thank you.

social.t: He has not returned to work. Offer a fit note, discuss a phased return and workplace adjustments, and signpost occupational health and financial advice if income is affected.
Family messages that he should “just be grateful” add to his distress. With his consent, explaining the syndrome to them can change the support he gets at home.

legal.t: A fit note can advise “may be fit for work” with a phased return or altered duties when he is ready (DWP fit note guidance).
If impairments are substantial and long-term, he may be protected under the Equality Act 2010, which requires reasonable adjustments at work.

professional.t: NICE CG83 expects a review 2 to 3 months after critical-care discharge. Recognise the gap without blaming colleagues, coordinate referrals, and record who is following what up.
Get his agreement before discussing his health with his family (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), ICUsteps peer support for ICU survivors and their families, and Samaritans for crisis support.

redFlags: Worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis or fever — possible lung complications or thromboembolism
Ongoing weight loss or swallowing problems
psychosocial: Off work with poor concentration; financial strain
Family telling him to be grateful; irritability at home
Sleep broken by nightmares; avoidance of hospital reminders
ice: Idea: “Something must still be wrong — or I’m weak”
Concern: guilt for struggling; fear it will never improve
Expectation: an explanation and to know if it gets better

playbook.diagnosis: Post-intensive-care syndrome after three weeks of ventilation for ARDS: physical (weakness, fatigue, exertional breathlessness), cognitive (memory and concentration) and psychological (low mood, probable PTSD) impairment, with no red flags reported and no post-discharge review.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Intensive care saves lives, but weeks on a breathing machine take a toll on the muscles, the memory and the mind. What you’re going through is a recognised after-effect, and each part has its own help.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you feel guilty for struggling. Being grateful and finding this hard can both be true — and asking for help is exactly the right thing.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and phased return plan; offer to explain the condition to his family; signpost peer support; prioritise sleep through treating the trauma symptoms.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination with SpO2; FBC, U&E, LFTs, thyroid function, glucose
PHQ-9 and GAD-7; referral for trauma-focused psychological therapy (NICE NG116)
Physiotherapy and graded reconditioning; critical-care follow-up service if available
Fit note now; cognitive strategies and a phased return to work later
safetyNet: Same-day contact for worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis or fever; 999 if severe
Review this week; GP tracks referrals

pitfalls.intro: Candidates fail this station by treating one symptom, echoing the “be grateful” message, or missing the trauma symptoms and suicide risk. The patterns below are fixable.

items.fail: Investigating fatigue with bloods alone and booking a review.
items.why: Post-intensive-care syndrome spans physical, cognitive and psychological domains. A single-domain plan earns little in Tasks.
items.fix: Name the syndrome and build a plan with a part for the body, the mind and concentration or work.

items.fail: Hearing “flashbacks” and never asking about nightmares, avoidance or suicidal thoughts.
items.why: PTSD and risk are core to this case. Missing risk is a safety failure.
items.fix: Ask about intrusions, avoidance and hyperarousal, and ask about suicide directly.

items.fail: Offering a benzodiazepine or sleeping tablet for the nightmares.
items.why: NICE NG116 advises against benzodiazepines for PTSD; they do not treat the disorder.
items.fix: Refer for trauma-focused CBT; mention venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline only if he prefers medication.

items.fail: Agreeing that he is lucky and should focus on the positives.
items.why: This repeats the invalidation driving his guilt and reads as not responding to the cue.
items.fix: Say it plainly: gratitude and suffering can coexist, and struggling is not weakness.

items.fail: Listing referrals without deciding which comes first or who follows them up.
items.why: He fell through a follow-up gap once already. A vague plan repeats it.
items.fix: Let him choose the first priority, and tell him you will chase the referrals and see him this week.

items.fail: Safety-netting only for mood or only for breathing.
items.why: Both physical and mental-health deterioration are possible here.
items.fix: Name the physical red flags and the crisis contacts in the same closing summary.

timeMap.d: He opens with the full list and the guilt. Let him finish; acknowledge it before questioning.
Physical function and red flags; flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance, mood and suicide risk; memory, concentration and work.
Where the guilt comes from (family); what he hopes for today.
Post-intensive-care syndrome; gratitude and suffering coexist; examination and bloods; therapy, physio, critical-care follow-up, fit note.
Physical red flags, crisis contacts, face-to-face this week, you chase referrals, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Treats fatigue alone with bloods; misses the flashbacks and never asks about suicide; agrees he should be grateful; no name for the problem; no referrals or follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Recognises post-intensive-care syndrome; screens physical, cognitive and psychological domains including risk; refers for therapy and physiotherapy; arranges review with basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: reframes the guilt explicitly; recognises the missed 2 to 3 month review; lets him set the first priority; offers to explain to his family; tracks referrals personally; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Well, you’re lucky to be here — it just takes time.”
avoid.instead: “Being grateful to be alive and finding this hard are both true. What you’re going through has a name, and there’s help for it.”
avoid.why: Repeats the invalidating message that stops him seeking help.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you something to help you sleep.”
avoid.instead: “The nightmares are part of trauma stress, and a specific talking therapy works best for that.”
avoid.why: NICE NG116 advises against benzodiazepines; sedatives do not treat PTSD.

avoid.instead: “Bloods, yes — and alongside them, help for your body, your mood and your concentration.”
avoid.why: A single-domain plan misses the syndrome.

SCA_STEM.recent: Discharged after three weeks of ventilation in ICU for severe pneumonia/ARDS five months ago. No follow-up clinic letter on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: still exhausted, weak and breathless on stairs, poor concentration, flashbacks and low mood.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG83 (rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, 2009) · NICE QS158 (2017) · NICE NG116 (post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New physical, cognitive and psychological problems after an ICU stay form post-intensive-care syndrome. Name it, screen each domain including PTSD and risk, and coordinate rehabilitation that should have started at the 2 to 3 month review.

points.t: NICE CG83: people with rehabilitation needs should have a functional reassessment 2 to 3 months after discharge from critical care, covering physical, psychological, social and sexual dimensions. If recovery is slower than expected or new problems arise, refer to rehabilitation or specialist services. He is five months out with no review.

ICU-acquired weakness, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, weight loss, and voice or swallow problems after intubation. Examine, check SpO2, and consider FBC, U&E, LFTs, thyroid function and glucose for other causes of fatigue. New or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, fever or weight loss need prompt assessment.
Depression, anxiety and PTSD are common after ICU. Use PHQ-9 and GAD-7 for mood and anxiety and ask about intrusions, nightmares, avoidance and hyperarousal. Ask about suicidal thoughts directly.

NICE NG116: offer individual trauma-focused CBT to adults with PTSD or clinically important symptoms more than a month after the trauma; EMDR is an option after non-combat trauma. If he prefers drug treatment, consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline. Do not use benzodiazepines.
Memory, attention and processing problems affect work and daily life. Assess impact, offer practical strategies, and plan a phased return to work with a fit note and occupational health.

NICE QS158 sets out follow-up after critical care discharge. Refer to a critical-care follow-up or rehabilitation service where one exists, physiotherapy for reconditioning, and psychological therapy. Track referrals rather than leaving them to chance.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him list all his symptoms and the guilt without interruption.
Work, family reactions, daily function and sleep.
Followed the flashbacks and the “I should be grateful” guilt.
Idea (weakness or something still wrong), concern (guilt, never improving), expectation (an explanation and hope).
Face-to-face examination with SpO2; FBC, U&E, LFTs, thyroid function, glucose; PHQ-9 and GAD-7.
PICS across three domains vs ongoing lung damage, anaemia, thyroid disease, depression and PTSD.
Asked about worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, fever, weight loss and suicidal thoughts.
Named post-intensive-care syndrome with probable PTSD in plain words.
Trauma-focused psychological therapy (NICE NG116), physiotherapy and reconditioning, critical-care follow-up referral, fit note and phased return.
Mood, sleep and cognition addressed; family offered an explanation; no benzodiazepines.
Face-to-face review this week, referrals tracked, physical red flags and crisis contacts named.

social.t: He has not returned to work. Offer a fit note, discuss a phased return and workplace adjustments, and signpost occupational health and financial advice if income is affected.
Family messages that he should “just be grateful” add to his distress. With his consent, explaining the syndrome to them can change the support he gets at home.

legal.t: A fit note can advise “may be fit for work” with a phased return or altered duties when he is ready (DWP fit note guidance).
If impairments are substantial and long-term, he may be protected under the Equality Act 2010, which requires reasonable adjustments at work.

professional.t: NICE CG83 expects a review 2 to 3 months after critical-care discharge. Recognise the gap without blaming colleagues, coordinate referrals, and record who is following what up.
Get his agreement before discussing his health with his family (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), ICUsteps peer support for ICU survivors and their families, and Samaritans for crisis support.

Ongoing weight loss or swallowing problems

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Post-intensive-care syndrome after three weeks of ventilation for ARDS: physical (weakness, fatigue, exertional breathlessness), cognitive (memory and concentration) and psychological (low mood, probable PTSD) impairment, with no red flags reported and no post-discharge review.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Intensive care saves lives, but weeks on a breathing machine take a toll on the muscles, the memory and the mind. What you’re going through is a recognised after-effect, and each part has its own help.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you feel guilty for struggling. Being grateful and finding this hard can both be true — and asking for help is exactly the right thing.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and phased return plan; offer to explain the condition to his family; signpost peer support; prioritise sleep through treating the trauma symptoms.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates fail this station by treating one symptom, echoing the “be grateful” message, or missing the trauma symptoms and suicide risk. The patterns below are fixable.

items.fail: Investigating fatigue with bloods alone and booking a review.
items.why: Post-intensive-care syndrome spans physical, cognitive and psychological domains. A single-domain plan earns little in Tasks.
items.fix: Name the syndrome and build a plan with a part for the body, the mind and concentration or work.

items.fail: Hearing “flashbacks” and never asking about nightmares, avoidance or suicidal thoughts.
items.why: PTSD and risk are core to this case. Missing risk is a safety failure.
items.fix: Ask about intrusions, avoidance and hyperarousal, and ask about suicide directly.

items.fail: Offering a benzodiazepine or sleeping tablet for the nightmares.
items.why: NICE NG116 advises against benzodiazepines for PTSD; they do not treat the disorder.
items.fix: Refer for trauma-focused CBT; mention venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline only if he prefers medication.

items.fail: Agreeing that he is lucky and should focus on the positives.
items.why: This repeats the invalidation driving his guilt and reads as not responding to the cue.
items.fix: Say it plainly: gratitude and suffering can coexist, and struggling is not weakness.

items.fail: Listing referrals without deciding which comes first or who follows them up.
items.why: He fell through a follow-up gap once already. A vague plan repeats it.
items.fix: Let him choose the first priority, and tell him you will chase the referrals and see him this week.

items.fail: Safety-netting only for mood or only for breathing.
items.why: Both physical and mental-health deterioration are possible here.
items.fix: Name the physical red flags and the crisis contacts in the same closing summary.
